headings.title: Levels of Prevention and the Role of Screening
headings.content:
Health screening falls under **secondary prevention**, aiming to detect diseases early before symptoms become severe. Understanding the broader context of prevention helps student nurses explain the value of check-ups to clients.

- **Primary prevention**: Stopping a disease before it ever starts, such as immunization or health education.
- **Secondary prevention**: Finding a disease early when it is easier to treat, such as blood pressure checks or cervical screening.
- **Tertiary prevention**: Managing long-term illness to prevent complications and improve daily living, such as stroke rehabilitation.

headings.title: Pre-Screening Client Education and Instructions
headings.content: Clear communication before a screening test ensures accurate results. Nurses must provide verbal and written instructions regarding fasting, medication holds, or activity restrictions. A common misconception among patients is that they can take all their regular morning pills with water before a fasting blood sugar test; nurses must clarify which drugs are permitted and which must be delayed.

headings.title: Physical and Psychological Preparation of the Client
headings.content: Preparing a client goes beyond lab instructions; it involves addressing their anxiety and physical comfort. Many patients experience **white-coat syndrome**, where their blood pressure spikes simply from being in a clinical environment. Nurses must allow a few minutes of quiet rest before taking baseline vital signs. Furthermore, ensuring the client has emptied their bladder before a pelvic or abdominal examination reduces discomfort and prevents distorted findings.

headings.title: Dietary, Medication, and Lifestyle Restrictions
headings.content: Different screenings require specific lifestyle modifications beforehand. For instance, occult blood stool tests require avoiding red meat and certain vegetables to prevent false-positive results. Similarly, cardiac stress tests require clients to avoid caffeine and heavy meals. Nurses must review the client's current home medication list to identify drugs that interfere with upcoming diagnostic procedures.

headings.title: Environment, Equipment, and Safety Setup
headings.content:
A well-prepared screening environment promotes client privacy, dignity, and accurate data collection. 

- **Privacy**: Use functioning curtains and doors to protect the client during physical checks.
- **Lighting**: Ensure adequate illumination for inspecting skin lesions or mucous membranes.
- **Equipment calibration**: Check that weighing scales, sphygmomanometers, and glucometers are functioning properly before use.
- **Infection control**: Clean all reusable surfaces and stethoscope membranes between clients with approved disinfectants.

headings.title: Informed Consent and Ethical Considerations
headings.content: Even though screening is voluntary, clients must understand what the procedure involves, its limitations, and potential follow-up needs before agreeing. Nurses play a key role in confirming that consent is truly informed rather than just signing a form. Ethical screening also requires ensuring confidentiality of results and protecting vulnerable clients from coercion in workplace or community screening drives.

headings.title: Post-Screening Care and Results Communication
headings.content: The screening process does not end when the test is completed. Clients need clear instructions on when and how they will receive their results. Nurses must provide immediate post-procedure care, such as offering a snack after a fasting blood draw or monitoring for bleeding after a finger-prick. Most importantly, abnormal results must be communicated promptly with clear pathways for further diagnostic confirmation.
